pages_convention: XML section and paragraph locators (jats_text) where the XML text holds the passage (abstract §0 ¶1 and captions such as Fig. 4). The XML holds no body text, so body passages are cited by printed journal pages (p. N), which equal PDF pages counted from 1. Figure-content steps cite the caption label plus the PDF page.

entry.evidence: This study examines the hypothesis that proglacial chemical weathering is associated with meltwater chemistry in the proglacial zone

sequences.source_document: Published paper PDF with XML abstract/captions

steps.action: Frames the gap: the effect of glacier recession on biogeochemical cycles is unclear, and chemical weathering rates along glacier-foreland chronosequences are little known.
steps.quote: the impact of glacier changes on biogeochemical cycles is unclear

steps.action: States the working hypothesis that proglacial chemical weathering is associated with meltwater chemistry during the early stage of recession.
steps.quote: This study examines the hypothesis that proglacial chemical weathering is associated with meltwater chemistry in the proglacial zone

steps.action: Uses the foreland as a space-for-time chronosequence: 23 samples from proglacial zone I (27–44 years), proglacial zone II (>60 years) and the LIA terminal moraine (>100 years), with exposure ages taken from front-position history.
steps.quote: Soil and sediment samples (N = 23) were collected along the chronosequence in front of Werenskioldbreen in three different areas

steps.action: Reuses the 2011 ablation-season meltwater ion chemistry and discharge data from the authors' earlier study (portal, two artesian outflows, and the hydrometric station).
steps.quote: Raw water chemistry data were obtained from earlier work (Stachnik et al., 2016)

steps.action: Characterizes the sediments by XRD mineralogy, SEM-EDS imaging of grain morphology and physical weathering, EDS point analyses (Table 2) and EDS line profiles of Fe sulphide grains and their Fe oxide rims.
steps.quote: Microcracks were common in calcite, quartz, and dolomite mineral grains

steps.action: Compares grains across the chronosequence and reads a progression from poorly weathered Fe sulphides in zone I, through advanced oxidation in zone II, to intense weathering in the moraine, with sulphur loss and oxygen gain in rims.
steps.quote: Along the proglacial chronosequence, weathering of Fe sulphides changed from being poorly weathered in proglacial zone I

steps.action: Checks the weathering trend with a second method: QEMSCAN quantitative mineralogy shows sulphide content falling from zone I to the moraine.
steps.quote: as shown by the results of the QEMSCAN® analyses (Fig. 7)

steps.action: Corrects ion concentrations for sea-salt input using seawater ion:Cl ratios, then computes the sulphate mass fraction and the silicate-to-carbonate cation ratio as weathering-process indicators (Table 3).
steps.quote: The SMF index showed generally higher values than 0.35 during the early and late parts of ablation season

steps.action: Checks the regression assumptions with Kolmogorov-Smirnov, Shapiro-Wilk and Durbin-Watson tests, log-transforms where residuals are non-normal, and cross-checks Pearson against Spearman correlations.
steps.quote: parametric (Pearson's, hereafter r) and non-parametric (Spearman's rank order, hereafter rho) correlation coefficients showed similar range of values

steps.action: Fits ion regressions by season and site; finds *Ca2++*Mg2+ versus SMF strong at the proglacial hydrometric station (r = 0.83) and weaker at the subglacial outflows (r ~0.5–0.6).
steps.quote: correlation coefficients between *Ca2++*Mg2+ and SMF were positive and strong for the hydrometric station

steps.action: Explains why sulphide oxidation and carbonate dissolution are more advanced in the younger proglacial zones than in the older moraine by invoking auxiliaries: finer grains, physical weathering and higher water saturation.
steps.quote: This is likely related with a smaller grain fraction in the sediments (higher specific surface area), physical weathering, and relatively higher water saturation

steps.action: Links the sulphur-depleted rims and carbonate loss in the sediments to the meltwater signal of sulphuric-acid carbonate dissolution at the proglacial station.
steps.quote: meltwater chemistry mimics sediment alteration because of a stronger coupling between carbonate derived ions

steps.action: Compares results with the earlier Werenskioldbreen data and other glacier studies; the silicate-to-carbonate cation ratio is an order of magnitude lower than in other metasedimentary basins, so carbonate weathering outweighs silicate weathering.
steps.quote: an order of magnitude lower than other glacierised basins underlain by metasedimentary rocks

steps.action: Keeps the claim that sulphide oxidation in proglacial sediments supplies sulphuric acid that drives carbonate dissolution seen in the meltwater, i.e. strong sediment–meltwater coupling.
steps.quote: the observations from the hydrochemistry are in line with our SEM-EDS results of sediments from the proglacial zone

steps.action: Extends the claim to iron: leaching of Fe-bearing minerals peaks in the first ~100 years, implying a larger early supply of reactive Fe downstream that declines with longer exposure.
steps.quote: leaching of Fe-bearing minerals and formation of iron hydroxide is strongest at the early stages of glacier recession (up to ~100 years)

tree.answer: Coupling of proglacial sediment weathering (sulphide oxidation, carbonate dissolution) with meltwater chemistry
Partly: grain weathering seen directly by SEM-EDS; coupling inferred from ion indices
Explain how sediment weathering shapes meltwater chemistry along a chronosequence
Implicit process rivals only: carbonation, sulphide oxidation coupled to carbonate dissolution, silicate weathering
Literature SMF thresholds (0.5) and cation ratios separate the processes; not derived here
Found: space-for-time foreland chronosequence and existing outflow samples

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: Repeated seasonal water samples at several outflows
Survives QEMSCAN cross-check, Spearman versus Pearson, and log transforms

end.claim: Combined hydrochemical, XRD and SEM-EDS evidence shows strong biogeochemical coupling between proglacial sediments and meltwater during the first ~100 years after deglaciation: sulphide oxidation supplies sulphuric acid that dissolves carbonates.

decisive_move.sentence: Without the comparison showing a strong *Ca2++*Mg2+–SMF correlation at the proglacial station relative to subglacial outflows, the sediment observations would not connect to meltwater chemistry, and the coupling claim would not exist.

gates.evidence: The hypothesis is stated (p. 2) and the chronosequence sediment sampling serves it, but the water data were collected in 2011 for an earlier study (p. 4). The correlations could have come out weak, yet no rival is given a decisive test; the SMF thresholds come from the literature. Nothing is reported as fixed in advance.

imports.item: SEM-EDS imaging, BSE/SE modes and EDS point and line analyses
Ion chromatography and certified reference materials (inherited)
Kolmogorov-Smirnov, Shapiro-Wilk and Durbin-Watson residual tests; Spearman rank correlation

novelty_claims.quote: Despite their great potential, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) techniques have rarely been applied to identify mineralogical transformations in the proglacial zone.
[...] a new approach by focusing on the influence of sediment geochemistry on meltwater chemistry at the early stage of glacier retreat
although a link to meltwater chemistry has rarely been addressed (Anderson et al., 2000)

limits: Source and locators: the XML text holds only the abstract and captions, so body passages are cited by printed page. No review file was supplied; the acknowledgement mentions two reviewers, but what changed is unknown, so there is no review sequence and tree question 9 is not coded. The sediment sampling date is not stated (inference: possibly linked to the 2012 Arctic Field Grant), and the water data (2011) come from the authors' 2016 paper. Process and statistics: the chronosequence assumes space-for-time without a test; the moraine has 2 profiles (QEMSCAN N=2), and no statistical test of between-zone differences is reported. Internal tension: Results describe more intense sulphide weathering at the moraine (p. 6), while Discussion says oxidation and carbonate dissolution are more advanced in the younger proglacial zones (p. 10); step 11 codes the auxiliary explanation. The text attributes 'proglacial zone I (profile 012)' (p. 7), though profile 012 is moraine. Sub-claims and their status: physical weathering enhances oxidation (best_explanation from images); the Fe supply to downstream ecosystems and the CO2 implications have status none (inference, since Fe in meltwater is not measured here). Coupling rests on correlation, with no causal or mass-balance test.

disagreements.target: Studies of subglacial weathering beneath the Greenland Ice Sheet (Graly et al., 2014; Moore et al., 2013)
disagreements.support: At Werenskioldbreen, carbonate dissolution by sulphuric acid dominates even though carbonates and sulphides are minor, whereas those studies found silicate weathering dominant.
disagreements.quote: whereas chemical weathering under subglacial conditions beneath the Greenland Ice Sheet showed a strong impact of silicate weathering

disagreements.target: Other glacierised basins underlain by metasedimentary rocks (Stachnik et al., 2014; Wadham et al., 2010b)
disagreements.support: The meltwater silicate-to-carbonate cation ratio here is an order of magnitude lower, and SEM-EDS shows no aluminosilicate dissolution.
disagreements.quote: an order of magnitude lower than other glacierised basins underlain by metasedimentary rocks
